profile.feeling: Summer, Israeli salad, the red of the market stalls.

examples.tr: I (m.) am cutting a tomato for the salad.
The tomatoes at the market are very fresh.
She is cooking tomato sauce for the pasta.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in use: the 1886 coinage won over its competitors.

etymology.text: Coined by early religious Zionist Yechiel Michel Pines in 1886, under the influence of German Liebesapfel (literally “love apple”), from the root ע־ג־ב relating to lust. The word’s sexual undertones made it initially controversial, but it outcompeted alternative suggestions by the 1940s.

funFacts: The name was modelled on German Liebesapfel “love apple”: its root ע־ג־ב is the root of lust and desire.
pitfalls: Feminine: עַגְבָנִיָּה טְעִימָה (not טָעִים); “one tomato” is עַגְבָנִיָּה אַחַת, with the number after the noun.
Everyday spelling without vowels has two yods: עגבנייה (עגבניה is the defective spelling).
subtleties: Before ע the article is הָ, because ע cannot take a dagesh: הָעַגְבָנִיָּה, הָעַגְבָנִיּוֹת.

profile.feeling: Kitchen tears, frying smells.

examples.text: צָרִיךְ לְטַגֵּן אֶת הַבָּצָל עַד שֶׁיַּזְהִיב.
examples.tr: You need to fry the onion until it turns golden.

examples.text: חִתּוּךְ בָּצָל מַדְמִיעַ לִי אֶת הָעֵינַיִם.
examples.tr: Cutting onion makes my eyes water.
Tulip bulbs are planted in autumn.

phrases.tr: and the onions and the garlic
phrases.meaning: the Egyptian foods the Israelites longed for in the desert

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic بَصَل (baṣal) and related to Aramaic בּוּצְלָא.

funFacts: Hebrew בָּצָל and Arabic بَصَل are the same Semitic word.
Onions are among the foods the Israelites missed from Egypt (Numbers 11:5).
pitfalls: The plural בְּצָלִים shortens the first vowel.
בָּצָל יָרֹק (green onion) is the spring onion — a separate word in this course.
subtleties: בָּצָל is also a plant bulb: בְּצָלִים שֶׁל צִבְעוֹנִים = tulip bulbs.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (construct phrase). Tokenized as one word (the engine matches multi-word lexemes first).

profile.feeling: Chips, mash, Hanukkah latkes.

examples.tr: I (m.) am peeling potatoes.
A kilo of potatoes, please.
At Hanukkah people eat potato latkes.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday short form (a blend of תַּפּוּחַ + אֲדָמָה), plural תַּפּוּדִים; often written תפו״ד

etymology.text: Calque of French pomme de terre (literally “apple of [the] earth”), like Dutch aardappel and others.

funFacts: The same image as French pomme de terre, Dutch aardappel and Austrian German Erdapfel: an “earth apple”.
pitfalls: A construct phrase: the plural changes only the first word — תַּפּוּחֵי אֲדָמָה.
Normative Hebrew puts the article on the second word: תַּפּוּחַ הָאֲדָמָה; in speech הַתַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה is very common.
Never shorten it to תַּפּוּחַ — that is an apple.
subtleties: The first noun is in the construct state (smikhut): all inflection happens on תַּפּוּחַ, the article goes on אֲדָמָה.

lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun; no plural in everyday Modern Hebrew (Wiktionary lists none).

profile.feeling: Strong smell, Mediterranean cooking.

senses.def: garlic (the plant and its bulb, as food)

examples.tr: You need two cloves of garlic.
I (m.) don’t like garlic.
There’s a smell of garlic in the kitchen.

phrases.tr: and the onions and the garlic
phrases.meaning: the Egyptian foods the Israelites longed for in the desert

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ṯūm-; cognate with Akkadian 𒋧 (šūmū), Aramaic תּוּמָא (tūmā), Arabic ثُوم (ṯūm).

funFacts: Arabic ثُوم (ṯūm) is the same word — as in the Lebanese garlic sauce toum; Hebrew ש regularly matches Arabic ث and Aramaic ת.
The Bible has a plural, הַשּׁוּמִים (Numbers 11:5); Modern Hebrew uses the singular as a mass noun.
pitfalls: A mass noun: “garlic” is singular — קָנִיתִי שׁוּם. Count cloves (שִׁנֵּי שׁוּם) or heads (רָאשֵׁי שׁוּם).
Same spelling and vowels: the determiner שׁוּם “any, no … at all” — אֵין לִי שׁוּם דָּבָר “I have nothing at all”.
subtleties: The article doubles the ש: הַשּׁוּם.

profile.feeling: Israeli salad, fresh and crunchy.

examples.text: אֲנִי מֵכִין סָלָט עִם עַגְבָנִיּוֹת וּמְלָפְפוֹנִים.
examples.tr: I’m making a salad with tomatoes and cucumbers.
The kids love pickles.
How much is a kilo of cucumbers?

synonyms.nuance: the Biblical word (Numbers 11:5); in Modern Hebrew קִשּׁוּא means zucchini!

etymology.text: From Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple; tree fruit”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).

funFacts: It is often wrongly linked to לָפַף (to wrap around) because of the twisting vines; it really comes from Greek μηλοπέπων — a word a Greek speaker will recognize.
pitfalls: Two פ: מְלָפְפוֹן (m’laf’fon).
With the article the מ takes a dagesh: הַמְּלָפְפוֹן.
subtleties: The Biblical cucumber word קִשּׁוּא now means zucchini — a classic ‘false friend’ inside Hebrew.

profile.feeling: A beloved staple of Israeli cuisine.

examples.text: אָכַלְנוּ חָצִיל עַל הָאֵשׁ עִם טְחִינָה.
examples.tr: We ate fire-roasted eggplant with tahini.
Grandma is frying eggplants.
The eggplants at the market were cheap today.

etymology.text: Coined by Abraham Lunz in 1831, adapted from Arabic حَيْصَل (ḥayṣal).

funFacts: The word is young: it was coined in the 19th century from Arabic.
pitfalls: Before חָ the article becomes הֶ: הֶחָצִיל — but הַחֲצִילִים in the plural.
subtleties: חָצִיל עַל הָאֵשׁ is roasted directly over a flame — a dish, not just a cooking method.

profile.feeling: Healthy everyday food.

examples.tr: Mom is grating carrot for the salad.
I bought a kilo of carrots at the market.
Fresh carrot juice, please.

phrases.tr: the method of the stick and the carrot

etymology.text: From Persian گزر (gazar, ‘carrot’).

funFacts: Arabic جَزَر (jazar) is the same Persian word.
pitfalls: גֶּזֶר (carrot) and the verb גָּזַר (to cut; to decree) share the letters גזר — read the vowels or the context.
subtleties: For food the singular is often used for the mass: קָנִיתִי גֶּזֶר = I bought carrots.

profile.feeling: Sweet, orange, comforting oven food.

examples.tr: She bakes sweet potatoes in the oven.
Sweet-potato soup is just right for winter.
At the market there is orange and white sweet potato.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in use: the loanword is the standard name.

etymology.text: Ultimately from Spanish batata, itself borrowed from Taíno batata. May have entered Hebrew through Arabic بطاطا.

funFacts: English “potato” comes from the same Taíno word batata — it first meant the sweet potato.
pitfalls: Not the potato: the potato is תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה, the sweet potato בָּטָטָה.
Feminine, plural with -וֹת: בָּטָטוֹת.
subtleties: A false friend with Levantine Arabic: there بطاطا (baṭāṭā) is the ordinary potato.

profile.feeling: Small green peas, children’s plates, the freezer.

senses.def: pea; peas (usually as a mass noun)

examples.tr: I (m.) am cooking rice with peas.
The baby loves peas.
I bought a bag of frozen peas.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word.

funFacts: Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of heredity by crossing pea plants.
pitfalls: Used as a mass noun: אֲפוּנָה = peas. The plural אֲפוּנִים is rare in everyday speech.
Feminine, but the plural ends in -ים: אֲפוּנָה → אֲפוּנִים (like דְּלַעַת → דְּלוּעִים).
subtleties: Before א the article is הָ: הָאֲפוּנָה.

profile.feeling: Green, iron-rich, pastry fillings.

examples.tr: I (m.) add spinach to the omelette.
She baked a spinach pie.
There’s fresh spinach at the market.

etymology.text: Compare Aramaic תִּרְדָּא.

funFacts: Like גֶּזֶר and סֶלֶק it is a “segolate” noun (pattern קֶטֶל): stress on the first syllable, TE-red.
pitfalls: A mass noun in the kitchen: תֶּרֶד = spinach. The plural תְּרָדִים exists but is rare.
subtleties: The article doubles the ת: הַתֶּרֶד.

profile.feeling: Crunchy and sharp, a salad garnish.

senses.def: a wet blanket, a dull person

examples.tr: I (m.) am slicing a radish for the salad.
The radishes in the garden are already big.
This radish is very sharp.

synonyms.nuance: the small red radish — the usual name for it in Israeli shops

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word.

funFacts: The plural keeps the o of the singular: צְנוֹן → צְנוֹנִים (tsnon → tsnonim).
pitfalls: The small red radish is usually called צְנוֹנִית; צְנוֹן is the general word and the larger radish.
subtleties: The article doubles the צ: הַצְּנוֹן.

profile.feeling: Autumn, soups.

examples.tr: Pumpkins are picked at the end of summer.
In winter I make pumpkin soup.
The children carved a face into the pumpkin.

synonyms.nuance: an alternative vocalization of the same word

etymology.text: Compare Arabic دَلَّاع (dallāʕ, ‘watermelon’).

funFacts: Its Arabic relative دَلَّاع means ‘watermelon’.
pitfalls: Feminine noun with a masculine-looking plural: דְּלַעַת → דְּלוּעִים.
subtleties: One Hebrew word for what English splits into pumpkin, gourd and squash.

profile.feeling: Crisp green leaves, sandwiches, the Seder plate.

senses.def: lettuce (the plant; its leaves as food)

examples.tr: I (m.) am washing the lettuce.
I bought two heads of lettuce at the market.
I put lettuce leaves in the sandwich.

etymology.text: From Aramaic חַסָּא (khassaʾ). Compare likely cognates Arabic خَسّ (ḵass) and Maltese ħassa, both with the same meaning.

funFacts: Many families use lettuce as the bitter herb (מָרוֹר) at the Passover Seder.
pitfalls: Homograph: חָסָה (with qamats) “took shelter”; the vegetable has patah and a dagesh: חַסָּה.
subtleties: Countable as heads (חַסּוֹת), a mass noun as food: סָלָט עִם חַסָּה.
ח cannot take a dagesh, so the article stays הַ without doubling: הַחַסָּה.

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (noun + adjective). Tokenized as one word (the engine matches multi-word lexemes first).

profile.feeling: Heat, tears, Yemenite and North-African kitchens.

examples.tr: He likes chili pepper in his pita.

examples.text: אַל תִּגַּע בָּעֵינַיִם אַחֲרֵי שֶׁחָתַכְתָּ פִּלְפֵּל חָרִיף!
examples.tr: Don’t touch your eyes after cutting chili!

examples.text: בַּשּׁוּק מוֹכְרִים פִּלְפְּלִים חֲרִיפִים יְרֻקִּים וַאֲדֻמִּים.
examples.tr: At the market they sell green and red chili peppers.

synonyms.nuance: the international loanword, common in speech and on menus

etymology.text: פִּלְפֵּל “pepper” (attested in Mishnaic Hebrew, from Classical Persian پلپل (pilpil), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”), likely via Aramaic) + חָרִיף “spicy, sharp” (possibly a borrowing from Aramaic).

funFacts: The Yemenite-Israeli hot sauce סְחוּג (s’khug) is made of chili peppers and coriander.
pitfalls: Both words agree and both take the article: הַפִּלְפֵּל הֶחָרִיף (the article is הֶ before חָ).
Plural on both words: פִּלְפְּלִים חֲרִיפִים — the qamats of חָרִיף shortens to a hataf patah, as in חָצִיל → חֲצִילִים.
subtleties: חָרִיף alone also means “sharp, harsh”: בִּקֹּרֶת חֲרִיפָה “harsh criticism”.

profile.feeling: Coleslaw, stuffed leaves, Eastern-European grandmothers.

examples.tr: I (m.) am shredding cabbage for a salad.
Grandma is cooking stuffed cabbage.

examples.text: בַּשּׁוּק יֵשׁ כְּרוּב לָבָן וּכְרוּב סָגֹל.
examples.tr: At the market there is white cabbage and purple cabbage.

etymology.text: From Ancient Greek κράμβη (krámbē, “cabbage”).

funFacts: A Greek speaker will recognize κράμβη in כְּרוּב; Arabic قَرْنَبِيط (cauliflower) comes from the same Greek word.
pitfalls: Homograph: כְּרוּב “cherub” (plural כְּרוּבִים) — the winged figures over the Ark.
After וּ the כ loses its dagesh: כְּרוּב לָבָן וּכְרוּב סָגֹל.
subtleties: Cauliflower כְּרוּבִית is built on this word: “little cabbage”.

profile.feeling: Roasted whole in the oven — a modern Israeli favourite.

examples.tr: We roast a whole cauliflower in the oven.
The children don’t like cauliflower.
How much is the cauliflower?

etymology.text: Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda from כרוב (“cabbage”) + ־ית, under influence of Arabic قَرْنَبِيط (qarnabīṭ), which itself was derived from Ancient Greek κράμβη (krámbē, “cabbage”).

funFacts: Ben-Yehuda, the reviver of spoken Hebrew, coined the word.
pitfalls: Feminine (ending ־ִית): כְּרוּבִית טְעִימָה; plural כְּרוּבִיּוֹת.
subtleties: The word is כְּרוּב “cabbage” + the ending ־ִית: a cabbage relative.

profile.feeling: Little green trees on a child’s plate.

examples.tr: He is steaming broccoli.
I bought frozen broccoli.
I (m.) add broccoli florets to the pasta.

etymology.text: From Italian broccoli (plural of broccolo, “cabbage sprout”); Wiktionary gives no separate Hebrew etymology.

funFacts: Italian broccoli is already a plural (“little sprouts”); Hebrew treats the word as a singular mass noun.
pitfalls: No plural: a mass noun, masculine — בְּרוֹקוֹלִי טָעִים. Count florets: פִּרְחֵי בְּרוֹקוֹלִי.
subtleties: Stress on the first syllable: BRO-ko-li.

profile.feeling: Soups, patties, Rosh Hashanah blessings.

examples.tr: Mum is cooking leek soup.
I (m.) wash the leek well.
At Rosh Hashanah people eat leek patties.

etymology.text: From Akkadian 𒂵𒆜𒊬 (GA.KASKAL^(SAR), GA.RAŠ^(SAR) /karašu/), from Sumerian 𒂵𒆜𒊬 (/garaš/). Also Aramaic כרתא / ܟܪܬܐ (karrāṯā), whence Arabic كَرَّاث (karrāṯ).

funFacts: A 4000-year-old word: Sumerian garaš → Akkadian karašu → Hebrew כְּרֵשָׁה.
Among the symbolic foods of the Rosh Hashanah meal the leek appears under its Aramaic name, כַּרְתִּי.
pitfalls: Feminine, but the plural ends in -ים: כְּרֵשִׁים.
Often spelled כרישה (with י) in everyday writing.
subtleties: The Biblical leek is חָצִיר (Numbers 11:5) — a word that means “hay” in Modern Hebrew.

profile.feeling: Red, yellow and green — the colours of Israeli salad.

senses.def: pepper, capsicum (the vegetable), especially the bell pepper

examples.tr: I (m.) am cutting a red pepper for the salad.
Grandma stuffs peppers with rice.
It needs a little black pepper.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word for a (red) bell pepper
“sweet pepper”, as opposed to פִּלְפֵּל חָרִיף (chili)

etymology.text: Attested in Mishnaic Hebrew, from Classical Persian پلپل (pilpil), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”), likely via Aramaic פלפל, פלפלא.

funFacts: The verb פִּלְפֵּל means “to pepper” and also “to debate at length” — hence פִּלְפּוּל, sharp Talmudic hair-splitting.
English pepper and Hebrew פִּלְפֵּל both go back to Sanskrit pippali.
pitfalls: One word for the vegetable and the spice: add a colour for the vegetable (פִּלְפֵּל אָדֹם) and שָׁחֹר for the spice.
subtleties: גַּמְבָּה, the everyday name of the red bell pepper, is according to Wiktionary supposedly a back-formation from גַּמְבּוֹת, a plural of Italian gambo “stem, stalk”.

profile.feeling: Deep red, stains everything.

examples.tr: I (m.) am cooking beetroot for the salad.

examples.text: הִיא שׁוֹתָה מִיץ סֶלֶק כָּל בֹּקֶר.
examples.tr: She drinks beet juice every morning.
The beetroot dyed my hands.

etymology.text: Compare Classical Syriac ܣܠܩܐ, Arabic سَلْق (salq).

funFacts: Among the symbolic foods of the Rosh Hashanah meal is beet (Aramaic סִלְקָא), a pun on יִסְתַּלְּקוּ “may (our enemies) depart”.
pitfalls: The plural shortens the first vowel: סְלָקִים.
Homograph without vowels: סִלֵּק “he removed; he paid off” (a verb).
subtleties: In the kitchen it is used as a mass noun: קָנִיתִי סֶלֶק = I bought beets.

profile.feeling: Summer gardens, stuffed vegetables.

examples.tr: I (m.) fry zucchini with onion.
A giant zucchini is growing in the garden.
In winter she cooks zucchini soup.

phrases.meaning: the foods of Egypt the Israelites longed for

etymology.text: Compare Arabic كوسة.

funFacts: In the Bible הַקִּשֻּׁאִים were cucumbers (Numbers 11:5); Modern Hebrew moved the word to the zucchini.
pitfalls: Everyday spelling with י: קישוא, קישואים.
Plural קִשּׁוּאִים.
subtleties: In Israel the usual קִשּׁוּא is the pale-green Middle-Eastern summer squash, not only the dark-green European zucchini.

profile.feeling: A green side dish, often in tomato sauce.

examples.text: אֲנִי מְבַשֵּׁל שְׁעוּעִית יְרֻקָּה בְּרֹטֶב עַגְבָנִיּוֹת.
examples.tr: I (m.) cook green beans in tomato sauce.
I bought fresh green beans.
The green beans are too soft.

synonyms.nuance: “beans” in general — without יְרֻקָּה it usually means the dried white beans

etymology.text: שְׁעוּעִית “bean” (Wiktionary gives no etymology) + יְרֻקָּה, feminine of יָרֹק “green” (from Proto-Semitic *waruḳ-; compare Arabic وَرَق, “leaf”).

funFacts: Hebrew יָרֹק “green” and Arabic وَرَق “leaf” come from the same Semitic root.
pitfalls: The adjective agrees with the feminine noun and takes the article too: שְׁעוּעִית יְרֻקָּה, הַשְּׁעוּעִית הַיְּרֻקָּה.
A mass noun: “green beans” is singular in Hebrew.
subtleties: Everyday spelling: שעועית ירוקה (with ו for the kubutz).

lexemes.note: A two-word lexeme (noun + adjective). Tokenized as one word (the engine matches multi-word lexemes first).

ref.src: Composed from the Wiktionary (kaikki.org) entries בָּצָל and יָרֹק (no entry for the phrase)

profile.feeling: Fresh green rings on salads and omelettes.

examples.tr: I (m.) am chopping spring onion for the omelette.
She adds spring onion to the salad.
At the market they sell a bunch of spring onions.

profile.synonymsNone: No one-word synonym in everyday use.

etymology.text: בָּצָל “onion” (cognate with Arabic بَصَل, baṣal) + יָרֹק “green” (from Proto-Semitic *waruḳ-).

funFacts: Exactly like English “green onion”: noun + colour adjective.
pitfalls: The adjective agrees and takes the article too: הַבָּצָל הַיָּרֹק; plural on both words: בְּצָלִים יְרֻקִּים.
subtleties: Usually a mass noun for the chopped herb; the plural is used for whole stalks.
Everyday spelling: בצל ירוק, בצלים ירוקים.

lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun; Wiktionary lists no plural.

profile.feeling: Soup greens; the first dip of the Seder.

senses.def: karpas — the vegetable dipped in salt water at the Passover Seder

examples.tr: I (m.) add celery to the soup.
He chops celery leaves for the salad.

examples.text: בְּלֵיל הַסֵּדֶר טוֹבְלִים כַּרְפַּס בְּמֵי מֶלַח.
examples.tr: On Seder night one dips karpas in salt water.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday loanword, especially for stalk celery

etymology.text: Compare Maltese karfus (“celery”), Classical Syriac ܟܪܦܣܐ (kerpəsā, “celery”), Arabic كَرَفْس (karafs, “celery”). The ultimate provenance of these terms is murky.

funFacts: A different word with the same letters: in Esther 1:6 כַּרְפַּס is a fine cotton fabric, from Sanskrit karpāsa “cotton”.
pitfalls: In everyday speech stalk celery is often called סֶלֶרִי; כַּרְפַּס is the standard word.
A mass noun: no plural in use.
subtleties: The Seder’s כַּרְפַּס need not be celery: families use parsley, celery or even potato.

lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun; Wiktionary lists no plural.

profile.feeling: Summer beaches, corn on the cob.

examples.text: בַּקַּיִץ אוֹכְלִים קְלַח תִּירָס עַל הַחוֹף.
examples.tr: In summer people eat corn on the cob at the beach.
I (m.) add corn to the salad.
I bought a bag of frozen corn.

etymology.text: After a son of Japheth (תִּירָס: Tiras) listed in Genesis 10 who was sometimes identified with the Turkish people, who have been traditionally considered as the main source of distribution of maize in Europe.

funFacts: Many languages wrongly credited maize to the East: Hebrew “Tiras” (= the Turks), Italian granturco (“Turkish grain”) — while Turkish calls it mısır, “Egypt”.
pitfalls: Normative stress is on the last syllable (tirás); in everyday speech many say TÍ-ras.
A mass noun: תִּירָס = corn. Count the cobs: קְלָחֵי תִּירָס.
subtleties: Also the name of the Biblical Tiras, son of Japheth (Genesis 10:2).
